steps.text:
Every endgame move, yours and your opponents', from your Lichess 3+2 and 5+0 games from mid-2024 through the 900-game block.

Small endgames (seven pieces or fewer, kings and pawns included) were checked against the endgame tablebase: a solved table, so “winning” and “mistake” there are facts. That was 18,209 moves from 857 games.

Bigger close endgames (neither side clearly winning) were re-checked with a stronger engine search than the one used on your games so far, which also counted how many moves were fine in each position. That was 38,466 moves from 2,005 games. A sample was checked again deeper still: 90% of the mistakes held up, the same for you and your opponents.

When the tablebase says you are winning, you let the win slip on 4.2% of moves. Your opponents, in the same spot, 4.8%.

When it is a draw and a losing move exists, you lose the draw on 9.1% of moves, they do on 10.0%.

The first time you reach a tablebase win in a game you go on to win 77% of the time; your opponents 80%. That difference is small enough to be chance.

What it means: king-and-pawn and simple rook endings are not where your endgame points go. The basic-technique drills are still worth a pass, but they are not the priority.

cards.t: Small endgames: you are as good as they are

steps.text:
In close endgames with eight or more pieces, you make a big mistake (a drop of 15 or more points of winning chance out of 100) on 12.2% of moves. Your opponents, in the same games, 10.3%. The stronger engine agrees with the earlier finding, and it holds in the 900-game block too (11.4% against 9.5%).

Where it is widest: rook endings (10.9% against 8.4%), bishop-and-knight endings (11.9% against 8.4%), pawn moves (13.5% against 10.7%), and any position with a passed pawn on the board, yours or theirs.

So your endgame gap starts while there is still a fair amount of wood on the board, and it is mostly gone by the time things are simple.

cards.t: Bigger endgames: the gap is real

steps.text:
In one position in five, only one move keeps the game. In more than half, lots of moves are fine.

You spend about the same time on both: a typical move takes 2 to 3 seconds either way. Your opponents do exactly the same. Neither of you notices the critical moments, and on only-move positions both of you go wrong about one time in five.

Thinking longer in the game does not show up as fewer mistakes, but that is partly because the hard positions are the ones that get thought about. The useful habit is upstream of thinking: noticing that this is a one-move position.

cards.t: Nobody spends more time when it matters

steps.text:
Compared with your opponents, about 435 extra mistakes over these games. About half of them, 225, came in positions where four or more moves were fine.

Low clock makes it sharp: with 20 seconds or less, in positions where lots of moves work, you go wrong on 11.0% of moves; your opponents with the same clock, 5.4%. With more time the gap shrinks to about a point and a half.

About a quarter of these mistakes leave something capturable. Most are quieter: a king or pawn step that lets their pawn or rook in. More of yours are king and pawn moves than theirs.

What it means: when the clock is short and nothing is going on, a quick safe move beats a quick active one. Before a king or pawn move, one look: what does it stop guarding?

cards.t: Half your extra mistakes come when lots of moves were fine

steps.text:
One move or many? Before each endgame move, a one-second sort: is something forcing going on (a check, a pawn race, a piece attacked, their passed pawn moving)? If yes, spend the time. If no, play a safe move and save the clock.

The decks: “One move or many?” trains the sort on your own positions: half are only-move spots you missed, half are spots where you spent 10 seconds or more and anything sensible was fine. “Win it or hold it” is your own small endgames where one to three moves kept the result, checked against the tablebase.

Then the passed-pawn deck and the rook-ending methods, because that is where the bigger-endgame gap is widest.
